newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian sugar seen in surplus until early 1997.
newsitem.headline: Russian sugar seen in surplus until early 1997.

text.p: Russia's sugar trade is in the doldrums, with neither white or raw imports profitable in an oversupplied market, but traders said on Tuesday they hoped demand would pick up early next year.
"There are no imports or very, very small imports of raw sugar at the moment," said a Sucden trader in Moscow.
"There is too much white and raw sugar on the market. It is not interesting to bring it in."
Mikhail Zharinov, head of marketing at major importer Alfa-Eko, said raw sugar deliveries could pick up as early as January, after Russian refineries finish processing this year's beet harvest.
"There are fewer traders left. Those who survive on this market now will be at the top soon," Zharinov said.
"Next year is likely to be better for importers and for producers, and more interesting price-wise."
Traders said any major raws or whites buying by Russia was unlikely until 1997.
The cost of bringing in a tonne of white sugar from Europe was about $500, above an average wholesale price in Russia of $456-459.
Traders said Russia's low sugar beet harvest this year of 16 million tonnes, far below last year's 19.1 million, could spur imports -- but no sooner than early next year.
"Poor beet harvests in Russia and Ukraine could help the market recover -- but we do not expect this to happen before the traditional time in February or March," said the Sucden source.

Industry sources said the government's consideration of a white sugar import quota of 1.5 million tonnes per year would not depress the market since the ceiling was high enough for most players to keep buying.
The number of sugar importers in Russia has slumped by two thirds over the past year to around 200 firms as low prices and high import duties forced many smaller traders out of business.

Sources said higher import duties and a 10 percent value-added tax on Ukrainian sugar had consolidated the market. Total Russian duties and taxes on imported raws were about 11 percent, compared with 36 percent on whites.
Zharinov said average monthly imports of white sugar from Ukraine fell sharply after Moscow last month slapped its value-added tax on Ukrainian raw and refined sugar imports.
Russian white sugar prices had been stable at $450-460 per tonne for months and traders said they would not slip lower.
But they expected Russia to continue bringing in raws under a long-term oil-for-sugar barter agreement with Cuba, despite quarreling between the two sides over terms.
"Russia has refineries working only on raw cane sugar, they have to keep up work, there must be imports," said one trader.

Government officials said importers of Cuban sugar for next year had yet to be approved, but traders noted Menatep-Impex and Alfa-Eko, both carrying out the most recent deal, were likely to continue their roles.

Russia planned to buy 2.5 million tonnes of raw sugar for the whole of 1996 and 1.0 million tonnes of white sugar, the latter mostly from Commonwealth of Independent States countries. About 1.5 million tonnes of the total for raws was covered by the barter deal with Cuba.
Russia last year imported 1.2-1.3 million tonnes of raws and about 1.8 million tonnes of white sugar.
At the same time Russia produced 2.0 million tonnes from its own beet crop.
The supplies covered annual demand of five million tonnes.
